Trust

The question you’re actually asking.

You read that your data stays on your computer. Then you noticed your agent thinks by sending your words to an AI company. So, do they read your email? Here is the whole answer, including the parts that don’t flatter us.

The awkward part, first

“You say my data stays with me. But my agent sends my email to an AI company, so they see it.”

Partly, yes, and we’d rather say it than have you find it. When your agent reads an email so it can summarize it, the text of that email goes to an AI model. That is what an AI agent is. Anyone who tells you their agent thinks without sending anything anywhere is selling you something that does not work.

So the honest question isn’t does anything leave. It’s whose account it goes under, and who is standing in the middle. Three answers:

1

It goes under your account, on your key.

You bring your own API key: a private access code from your AI company that lets Archie connect on your account. You pick which company, from Anthropic, OpenAI, Google, Groq or xAI, and you can change it later. The agent’s requests are billed to you and governed by your agreement with them, not ours. You are their customer, not our product.

2

We are not in the middle of it.

Archie calls the AI company directly from your computer. Not relayed through us. Not proxied by us. There is no Otian server in that path at all, so there is simply nothing on our side that could read it.

3

They don’t train on it.

Most of the AI companies Archie connects to state plainly that they do not train their models on API traffic. That is their commitment, not ours to make on their behalf, so don’t take our word for it. Each provider’s own words, the exceptions included, and a link to its source, are further down this page.

One exception, and it is ours. Archie starts you with a small amount of free credits so you can watch an agent work before being asked for an account of your own. Those run on Claude, on our Anthropic account, and that is the one case where your messages pass through a server of ours on the way. It works that way because there is no such thing as a personal key we could hand you: the alternative is our own key sitting inside the app on your laptop, where anyone could take it. Nothing about those messages is written down there. What the server records is how much was spent, so it can stop at the amount you were given. The moment you connect an account of your own, that path is gone and nothing of yours reaches us again.

What running on your own computer actually buys you, then, is this: your life does not also accumulate on a server of ours. There is no Otian archive to be breached, subpoenaed, sold in an acquisition, or quietly repurposed when our business model changes. We didn’t promise not to look at your data. We built it so there is nothing to look at.

One more thing you didn’t ask. If your agent searches the web, that search runs on the AI company’s own servers and is billed to your key, so your search query reaches their search backend, not just their model. Still not us.

In their own words

The one part of this that isn’t in our hands is what your AI company does with what you send it. So here is each provider Archie can connect to, on the record about training on API traffic. We quote the exact line where the provider lets us pull it, and link you straight to the source where it doesn’t. Every entry links out, and all were checked in August 2026.

  • Anthropic (Claude)
    “Anthropic may not train models on Customer Content from Services.”
    Commercial Terms of Service
  • OpenAI (ChatGPT)

    OpenAI’s API data usage policy states that content sent through its API is not used to train its models by default, and is retained for up to 30 days.

    Read it directly: OpenAI API data usage policies
  • Google (Gemini)
    “Google doesn’t use your prompts (including associated system instructions, cached content, and files such as images, videos, or documents) or responses to improve our products.”
    This is the paid tier, which is what your own API key uses. Google’s free tier does train on what you send. Gemini API Additional Terms of Service
  • Groq
    “Groq is not permitted to use Inputs or Outputs for training or fine-tuning any AI Model Services or other models, unless explicitly granted permission or instructed by Customer.”
    Groq Services Agreement
  • xAI (Grok)

    xAI is the one to check for yourself. Its enterprise terms commit not to train on customer content, but the consumer Grok app trains on conversations by default, so which set of terms applies depends on how your account is set up.

    Read it directly: xAI Privacy Policy and Enterprise Terms

Everything that leaves your computer.

Not a summary. Not the highlights. Every single thing Archie sends anywhere, what is in it, and who receives it.

Every outbound connection Archie makes, its destination, its contents, and whether it contains your content.
What Where it goes What’s actually in it Your content?
Your agent thinking Your AI company: directly, never through us The real thing: your prompt, the conversation, and whatever file, message, or transcript the agent is working with. Yes

It is scrubbed for anything secret-shaped before it is written, so the copy we get is the copy you can read yourself. At most five per launch, and nothing older than a week is sent at all. You can turn this off in the app, under Account, with the same switch that stops crash reports. None

If you find something Archie sends that is not on this list, that is a bug in our honesty and we want to know. Tell us, publicly, if you like.

Our servers

Everything our servers hold.

What we hold

  • Your email address, so you can sign in
  • Whether you have a current plan
  • Which paid add-ons you’ve bought
  • Which version of Archie you are running, until you turn that off
  • If you turn on phone access, the messages between your computer and your phone, sealed with a key we never receive

What we don’t

  • Your prompts and your agent’s replies. While you are on free credits they pass through our server on the way to Anthropic, and nothing there writes them down
  • Your files, notes, and knowledge base
  • Everything your agent remembers
  • Your calendar, emails, and messages
  • Your API keys
  • A record of which free add-ons you use
  • Anything about how you use Archie: what you open, what you run, how often

This list used to be three items long and called itself the whole list. Two of the things on it now arrived afterwards, and the old sentence stayed up for a while, which is how a true claim becomes a false one. The list is the claim, and the day something joins it is the day it appears here.

No company publishes this section

Where we fall short.

Every privacy page tells you what a company is good at. Here is the other half. If any of this changes, we will change it here on the same day.

Your agent asks before it changes anything, and that only helps if you read before you approve.

When your agent wants to change a calendar you’ve connected or send an email, it proposes the exact action and carries it out only after you approve that specific one, enforced in the app itself rather than by politely instructing the AI. The gate cannot stop it from proposing the wrong thing: if it misreads you and you approve without looking, it will carry out the mistake faithfully.

Two things it cannot do at all: it cannot spend money or buy anything, and it can only ever message you. The full version →

Untrusted text can reach your agent, and the gate won’t fully fix it.

If your agent reads a Slack attachment, a meeting transcript or a web page, a hostile message hidden in it could try to talk your agent into something you never asked for. The approval gate stops that from changing anything. It does not stop it from leaking something: a hostile instruction could still get your agent to run a web search whose query carries information from your conversation.

We don’t have a complete answer to that yet. Nobody in this industry does. The full version →

Archie checks your plan, and it tells you exactly what that check sees.

The app checks your plan when you sign in, so it isn’t a fully offline product, and we’re not going to dress that up: our servers see that your account has a current plan, and nothing more.

If we disappear, Archie keeps working. Our Terms require us to publish a final version that needs no sign-in at all, within 30 days of ceasing operations. That is a term of the agreement, not a promise on a blog. If you stop your plan, Archie stops letting you in at the end of the period you paid for, and nothing on your computer is deleted. The full version →

We keep a receipt for every paid add-on.

Buy a paid add-on and we store a permanent record: which one, how much, and when. It’s how we know to let you re-install it on a new computer. But it does mean we know which paid add-ons you own.

A free add-on leaves no receipt. Adding one bumps its public install count, signed in as you so the tally can’t be gamed, but we keep no record of which free add-ons are yours.

Nobody has audited us but us.

We have no third-party penetration test and no SOC 2 report. We’re a two-person team, and we’re saying so up front: you deserve to know exactly where we stand before you trust us with anything.

What we can offer instead is below: don’t trust us. Check.

Don’t trust us

Check for yourself. It takes 10 minutes.

Everything above this line is a claim, and claims are cheap. Here is how to prove or disprove ours without taking our word for a single thing.

1

Install a network monitor.

LuLu is free and open-source. Little Snitch is paid and friendlier. Either one shows you every connection an app on your Mac tries to make, and lets you block them.

2

Open Archie and use it properly.

Sign in. Install an add-on. Give your agent a real task: something with a file, or your calendar. Let it run. Then read the list of connections it made.

3

Here is exactly what you should see.

Your AI company, on your key, or our billing service standing in for it while you are still spending the free credits. Our sign-in and plan check, carrying your account ID. One update check to us, carrying nothing about you. Plus whichever accounts you connected, reached directly. If you see anything else carrying your content, we have either lied to you or made a serious mistake, and we want to hear about it either way. The exact hostnames to expect →

4

Now block us, and watch nothing happen.

Add otianai.com and archie-4f35.onrender.com to your firewall’s block list and keep working. Once your own key is in, your agent carries on exactly as before. That is the entire argument on this page, reduced to something you can test in thirty seconds: on your own key, nothing of ours is in the path, so cutting us out of it changes nothing. Try it before you connect a key and the free credits stop instead, because that one path really does run through us.

Where we think this ends up. The real answer to “why should I believe you” is an open-source client, so that none of this rests on our word. We’re not there yet, and we’re not going to describe a plan as though it were a fact. Read the long version of everything on this page →

The marketplace

An add-on is a text file, not a program.

The frightening version of a marketplace is: you install a stranger’s plugin, and it runs code on your computer, next to your email. That is not what this is, and the reason is structural, not a promise.

Archie has nowhere to run code. A Skill is a text file plus some settings. A Personality is a set of written instructions. A Routine is a schedule. Nothing in an add-on can run as a program, so it cannot read files off your disk on its own and cannot ship your data to a stranger’s server. Not because we’d catch it. Because there is no mechanism for it to use.

What an add-on can do is tell your agent how to behave and declare which of your connected accounts it needs. Today that is blunter than we want: declaring “calendar” grants reading, creating and deleting together, rather than asking you about each. How that works, in full →

Every add-on is read by a human before it is listed. Right now that human is one of the two of us, and we read every line of every submission. That will not scale forever. When it stops being true, this paragraph will change; we won’t quietly leave it here.
